summary: Explains what the IPFIX flow export protocol is good for, showing how different applications can use it and which information elements they would rely on. It also discusses the protocol's limits and how it relates to other measurement frameworks.

plainLanguage.summary: IPFIX is a way for network gear to send reports about the traffic it sees. This memo is the owner's guide: it says which jobs the tool suits, which it does not, and how it compares with other ways of measuring the same traffic.

subtitle: What the IPFIX flow export protocol suits, where it falls short, and how it compares with other measurement frameworks.

tldr.problem: IPFIX is a general protocol for exporting IP flow information, but operators need to know which applications it fits and what it cannot do.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through accounting, traffic profiling, traffic engineering, security, QoS monitoring and more, naming the Information Elements each needs, with a worked example of a template and its records. It then compares IPFIX with PSAMP, RMON, IPPM, AAA and RTFM and lists the limitations.
tldr.outcome: IPFIX is a good fit for flow-based measurement, but as specified then it did not meet the reliability needed for usage-based billing and had no standard remote configuration.

today: RFC 5472 is an Informational document published in March 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its limitation statements, such as the lack of standard remote configuration, describe IPFIX as of that time. The protocol itself is specified in RFC 5101 and the information model in RFC 5102.

sections.title: What IPFIX Is and What This Document Adds
sections.content:
The IPFIX protocol defines how IP Flow information can be exported from routers, measurement probes or other devices. That information is important input for a variety of applications, and the protocol is a general data transport that is easily extensible to suit their needs. This document describes how typical applications can use it, shows the opportunities and limitations of the protocol, and describes its relationship to other frameworks and architectures. Although the examples are shown for IPv4 only, the applicability statements apply to both IPv4 and IPv6, and IPFIX provides appropriate Information Elements for both.

The target applications and the requirements that come from them are described in the IPFIX requirements document, and those requirements were the basis for the design of the protocol. This document then shows how those target applications can use the protocol, and points to the section on limitations for the case of applications outside that list.
sections.plainLanguage: IPFIX is a way for network equipment to send reports about the traffic it sees. This memo is the guide to using it: which jobs it fits, which information each job needs, and where it falls down.

sections.title: Accounting and a Worked Example
sections.content:
Usage-based accounting is one of the target applications. IPFIX records provide fine-grained measurement results for flexible usage reporting, but IPFIX does not provide the reliability that usage-based billing systems require, so the accounting scenarios described here provide only limited reliability and should not be used where that reliability is mandatory.

To do accounting with IPFIX, the flow definition has to be chosen to suit the purpose, such as trend analysis, capacity planning, auditing, or billing and cost allocation where some loss of data can be tolerated. Flows can be distinguished by various Information Elements, and because the flow definition is flexible, arbitrary flow-based accounting models can be realized without extending the protocol. Accounting can be based on individual end-to-end flows, with a flow definition determined by the quintuple of source address, destination address, protocol and the two port numbers, or it can be class-dependent, as in a Diffserv network, where flows are distinguished just by the Diffserv codepoint and the two IP addresses. The essential elements are the number of packets and bytes per flow, represented by the per-flow counter Information Elements.

The worked example monitors individual flows in a Diffserv network so that traffic trends can be compared with the terms of a service level agreement. Flows are distinguished by source and destination address, and the information to export is the IPv4 source address, 4 octets long; the IPv4 destination address, 4 octets; the Diffserv codepoint, 1 octet; and the number of octets in the flow, 4 octets. The template set has Set ID 2 and a length of 24 octets, Template ID 256 and a field count of 4, and the four fields carry the Information Element numbers and lengths just listed. The sample records use the Diffserv codepoint 46, which is recommended for the Expedited Forwarding per-hop behaviour, and addresses from the example block, which is divided into two networks by subnetting with a 25-bit netmask.
sections.plainLanguage: Billing is the first job. You choose what makes a flow, for instance the address pair and the port pair, and count the packets and bytes in each one. The example shows the form of the records: a header that says which fields follow, then one record per flow with the address pair, the service class and the byte count.

sections.title: Profiling, Engineering, Security and Quality of Service
sections.content:
Traffic profiling. Records captured over a long period can be used to track and anticipate network growth and usage, which is valuable for trend analysis and network planning. The parameters of interest depend on the objective: flow duration, flow volume, burstiness, the distribution of services and protocols in use, and the number of packets of a specific type. The distribution of services and protocols can be analyzed by configuring the right flow keys, with protocols distinguished by the protocol identifier and port numbers often giving information about the services in use. Packet payload can be reported using the payload section element, flow duration can be calculated from the flow timestamp elements, and burstiness from the flow volume measured at different intervals.

Traffic engineering. This aims at optimizing network resource utilization and traffic performance. Typical parameters are link utilization, load between specific network nodes, the number, size and entry and exit points of active flows, and routing information. The size of flows can be reported with the packet and octet counters, and the utilization of a physical link with a coarse-grained flow definition based on interface identifiers. The load between specific nodes can be reported the same way if one interface of a node receives traffic from exactly one neighbour; otherwise, source MAC address can be added as a flow key. The total number of flows exported since the last initialization gives a running count, so the number of active flows in an interval is the difference between two readings, provided the termination criteria are taken into account. Neither the standard information model nor the packet-sampling one defines elements suitable for exporting routing information.

Network security. Attack and intrusion detection are target applications. The number of metrics useful for detection is as diverse as the attack patterns, and attackers adapt quickly and try to hide with slow or stealth attacks; unusual traffic is also often not malicious, since a sudden increase may be legitimate users fetching newly published content, and strange patterns may come from misconfiguration. IPFIX can export flow information for arbitrary flow definitions, and with the additional packet elements all information about traffic at the IP layer and above is accessible, either to detect anomalies directly or as the basis for further processing. A sudden increase in traffic load can hint at an attack; a sudden increase in flows from many sources to one destination may be an attack using spoofed addresses; many flows to the same machine on different ports, or to the same port on different machines, may indicate vertical or horizontal port scanning; and an unusual ratio of TCP SYN to TCP FIN packets can refer to SYN flooding. Worms may leave signatures in traffic patterns, which needs more detailed measurement and post-processing. Separating good from bad packets to prepare a counteraction may require a deeper look at packet content. The resources needed grow with the granularity required, so metrics should be chosen to give solid detection with minimal resource consumption, using coarser flow definitions, pre-processed metrics or sampling. Capturing full packet traces at every observation point is not viable because of resource limits and privacy concerns. Only derived metrics often provide sufficient evidence: comparing the number of SYN and FIN packets over an interval can reveal an ongoing attack that is not obvious from the raw data. Pre-processing at the measurement device speeds up detection and reduces what has to be exported, and the push model lets data be exported immediately when an incident is suspected, though extra exporting criteria are needed to export on incident detection and not only on flow end or fixed intervals.

Quality of service monitoring. This is the passive observation of transmission quality for single flows or traffic aggregates, for example to validate the guarantees in a service level agreement. Typical parameters are loss, one-way and round-trip delay, and delay variation, and the IP Performance Metrics definitions should be used when reporting them. Calculating them requires per-packet processing, which is possible by treating a single packet as a flow, and the packet-sampling document defines useful additional elements for this.

Some quality of service metrics need data from several observation points, which requires synchronized clocks and a way to recognize that the same packet was seen in more than one place. That can be done by capturing parts of the packet that do not change on the way, and to reduce the amount of data a unique packet identifier can be calculated from the content, using a cyclic redundancy check or a hash function instead of transferring the raw content; the hash value element can carry such an identifier. Header fields that can change on the way must be excluded from the identifier, and the amount of content used affects the collision rate.

Inter-domain exchange of IPFIX data with neighbour providers needs more care than use within one domain: the threat level is higher, so TLS or DTLS should be used, and the transfer should be congestion-aware, which means transport over SCTP or TCP. Some providers are reluctant to share information because competing providers might exploit it, but technical needs have already triggered such exchange in the past, as with routing information exchanged by BGP, and the need to defend networks against denial-of-service attacks and worms may increase the willingness to cooperate. IPFIX can also carry derived metrics directly, for example when the calculation sits alongside the metering and exporting processes, which requires additional Information Elements to be defined, and for most quality of service metrics the standard IP Performance Metrics definitions should be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The same records can answer a lot of questions: what is the network growing into, which links are busy, is something odd happening, and is the promised quality of service actually being delivered. The last two need care, because the more detail you ask for, the more work and bandwidth the measuring costs, and because unusual traffic is often not an attack at all.

sections.title: How IPFIX Compares with Other Frameworks
sections.content:
IPFIX has been designed for IPv4 and IPv6 from the beginning, so it can be used in either without limitation. Generating and reporting records about IPv6 traffic is possible with the appropriate elements, and exporting records over IPv6 only needs the chosen transport protocol to run in the IPv6 network.

PSAMP defines packet selection methods and the reporting of packet information, and uses IPFIX as a basis for exporting it. The main difference is that IPFIX addresses the export of flow records while PSAMP addresses the export of packet records, and PSAMP explicitly addresses remote configuration with a MIB for configuring packet selection processes, something IPFIX does not yet address.

RMON is a widely used monitoring system that gathers traffic data from agents in network devices. A major difference is that RMON uses SNMP for data export while IPFIX defines its own push-oriented protocol, and RMON defines MIBs holding the information to be exported while IPFIX defines it as Information Elements. The RMON transaction concept differs from the IPFIX flow concept: a transaction is service-oriented and describes the data exchange from a service request to its completion, while a flow is a generic term for grouping IP packets by common properties. Reporting the same thing with IPFIX would need a specific combination of multiple flows mapped to the transaction, and some RMON metrics, such as service responsiveness, are not addressed in IPFIX at all. The transport performance metrics MIB breaks transactions into sub-application level transactions, which for a web request would be DNS, TCP and HTTP, and such sub-transactions can be considered bidirectional flows, so with a suitable flow definition and the ability to map both directions they could be measured with IPFIX.

IPPM metrics can be carried by IPFIX, or the information needed to calculate them can.

AAA defines a protocol and architecture for authentication, authorization and accounting, with DIAMETER used for the communication, and it is used to transfer accounting records. Data from the network is needed to form accounting records for usage-based accounting, and IPFIX defines how to export such data, so connecting the two looks promising. The cooperation is valuable: flow records can provide the input for AAA accounting functions and the basis for generating DIAMETER accounting records, and coupling the collecting process with AAA functions can help identify the source of malicious traffic and deny access to suspicious users or nodes. Two ways of connecting them are described, one where a AAA client runs on the IPFIX collector and generates DIAMETER accounting messages, and one where an application specific module sits between the IPFIX protocol and the AAA server and translates the data. Neither requires changes to IPFIX or DIAMETER, although carrying IPFIX records inside DIAMETER would need new attribute value pairs, since the DIAMETER ones do not cover all IPFIX elements.

RTFM is very similar in architecture, defining a meter, a meter reader and a manager, with the manager configuring the meter and the reader collecting data, all over SNMP. The IPFIX architecture defines metering, exporting and collecting processes, speaking about processes rather than devices so that several may sit on one machine, and the definitions do not contradict each other. One difference is that IPFIX does not define a managing process, because remote configuration was initially out of scope. Both consider a flow to be a group of packets sharing common properties, completely specified by the set of values and a termination criterion, but RTFM defines flows as bidirectional and keeps two sets of counters, while IPFIX does not state either way and the elements describing flow properties are defined for one direction only. RTFM configures a meter remotely as the only way, using SNMP and a meter MIB. The data collection model differs most: RTFM retrieves data in pull mode over SNMP, where the security on the meter decides whether a reader may pull, while IPFIX uses a push model, with the exporting process configured to export to a list of collecting processes and the export condition configured in the exporting or metering process. RTFM uses continuously incrementing 64-bit counters that are never reset, and IPFIX allows both absolute counters that behave that way and delta counters that are reset when the record is exported. RTFM needs a reliable transport, so its reader must time out and resend unanswered SNMP requests, which is clumsy and limits the transfer rate. IPFIX is designed to work over a variety of transports, with SCTP and PR-SCTP mandatory and UDP and TCP optional, and encodes data much more efficiently than SNMP, so it has lower overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: There are other ways to measure the same traffic. Some ask the equipment for numbers, while IPFIX makes the equipment send reports on its own. Some group packets one way only, some both ways. Some can be configured remotely, some cannot. And IPFIX moves the data more efficiently than the older, SNMP-based scheme.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content:
The document is candid about what IPFIX cannot do. The reliability requirements of the IPFIX requirements document are not sufficient for usage-based billing as described in the accounting management document. IPFIX does not support resilience against record loss, except when TCP or SCTP carries the records; it does not demand the use of multiple collectors for fault tolerance, even though it allows one exporter to have several; it does not support detecting and eliminating duplicate records; and it does not support application layer acknowledgements, which would be needed to tell an exporter that the application cannot process the data it exported. Archival accounting and pre-authorization are outside the scope of the specification but have to be realized in the billing system architecture.

SCTP is the preferred transport and a conforming implementation must work over it, and although IPFIX can also work over TCP or UDP both have drawbacks, so users should have good reasons before choosing something else in a specific environment.

IPFIX works in push mode, so records are exported automatically without waiting for a request, and the responsibility for initiating an export lies with the exporting process, with the export criteria configured there. Push mode has more benefits when the trigger is an event at the exporting process, such as the end of a flow or a memory shortage, and it lets data be sent before a memory shortage forces data to be discarded. Exporting can also prevent overloading the exporting process by exporting as soon as thresholds are about to be exceeded, so the criteria are often tied to traffic characteristics or resource limits. But traffic characteristics are usually dynamic and often impossible to predict, so if they trigger the export, the exporting rate and the resource consumption become variable and unpredictable. Pull mode has advantages when the trigger is an event at the collecting process, such as an application asking for immediate input: a request could simply be forwarded to the exporting process, whereas in push mode the configuration has to be changed, and pull mode prevents the collecting process being overloaded by more records than it can process.

The IPFIX specification limits the template identifiers that can be assigned in an observation domain: identifiers up to 255 are reserved for template or option sets, and identifiers from 256 to 65535 are assigned to data sets, so an installation with many exports needing many different templates could exhaust the range.

On bidirectional flows, although IPFIX does not say explicitly that flows are unidirectional, the elements describing flow characteristics are defined for one direction only. The protocol allows reporting multiple identical elements in one record, so forward and reverse elements can go in one record, but that requires an agreement on the semantics, such as the first counter being the forward direction. The alternative is to use two adjacent records for the two directions, which needs extra means of mapping them and is inefficient because the flow keys are reported twice.

Finally, remote configuration was initially out of scope for the working group so that it could concentrate on the protocol specification, so there is currently no standardized way to configure IPFIX processes remotely, although the broad need for the feature makes it likely that solutions will be standardized soon.
sections.plainLanguage: The limits are worth knowing. Reports can be lost, duplicated or never acknowledged, so this is not a bank-grade ledger. There is no standard way to reconfigure the collectors remotely, and the identifiers used for record formats can run out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document describes the use of IPFIX in various scenarios. The security requirements for the target applications and the security considerations for IPFIX itself are addressed in the IPFIX requirements and IPFIX protocol documents, and those requirements have to be met for the use of IPFIX in all the scenarios described here. For inter-domain exchange, the document has already noted that the threat level is higher when data travels over the public Internet, that protection against disclosure or manipulation of data matters even more than within one domain, and that TLS or DTLS should be used.

Two further points follow from the applications themselves. Using IPFIX for accounting or for attack detection raises the incentive to attack IPFIX itself, since an attack that creates many flows, for example with spoofed addresses, can overload the exporting and collecting processes, and sampling can help. Combining IPFIX with AAA functions adds a hazard of its own, because where a collector or application specific module becomes a transit point for AAA traffic, the security mechanisms such as message encryption have to be maintained.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the reports are valuable, attackers may go after the reporting itself, so keep the links private and do not let a flood of fake traffic drown the system.
